name: biology_set1_p1
label: Biology: set 1 (cells, nutrition, respiration, transport, ecology and genetics)

papers.title: Characteristics of Living Things: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on characteristics of living things, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A seedling on a windowsill bends towards the light. Which characteristic of living things does this show?
questions.explanation:
Bending towards light is a response to a stimulus (light), so it shows irritability, also called sensitivity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Growth: Growth is a permanent increase in size; bending towards light is a response to a stimulus.
- Reproduction: Reproduction is producing new individuals, which is not happening here.
- Excretion: Excretion is removing the waste products of metabolism.

questions.stem: The removal of the waste products of metabolism from the body of an organism is called
questions.explanation:
Excretion removes waste made by the body's own chemical reactions, such as carbon dioxide and urea.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- egestion: Egestion removes undigested food, which was never part of the body's metabolism.
- secretion: Secretion releases useful substances such as enzymes and hormones, not wastes.
- respiration: Respiration releases energy from food; its waste, carbon dioxide, is then excreted.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of living things but NOT of a burning candle?
questions.explanation:
A flame uses oxygen and gives out energy and carbon dioxide, much like respiration, but it cannot produce offspring.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Use of oxygen: A burning candle also uses oxygen.
- Release of energy: A burning candle also releases energy, as heat and light.
- Production of carbon dioxide: Burning wax also produces carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: In the memory aid MRS GREN for the characteristics of living things, the letter N stands for
questions.explanation:
MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- nervous system: Not every living thing has nerves; MRS GREN lists features shared by all living things.
- nitrogen fixation: Only some bacteria fix nitrogen, so it is not a feature of all living things.
- natural selection: Natural selection is a process of evolution, not a feature of a single organism.

questions.stem: Growth in living things is best described as
questions.explanation:
Growth is an irreversible increase in size and dry mass, as new materials are built into the body.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a temporary swelling caused by taking in water: Swelling from water can be reversed; growth is permanent.
- an increase in the number of offspring: Producing offspring is reproduction.
- a change in the position of the whole organism: A change of position is locomotion.

options.label: A
options.content: a permanent increase in size and dry mass

options.label: B
options.content: a temporary swelling caused by taking in water

options.label: C
options.content: an increase in the number of offspring

options.label: D
options.content: a change in the position of the whole organism

questions.stem: A green plant takes in carbon dioxide and water and uses light energy to make glucose. Which characteristic of living things does this show?
questions.explanation:
Nutrition is the taking in or making of food. Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis (autotrophic nutrition); animals take in ready-made food.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Respiration: Respiration releases energy from food such as glucose; it does not make the food.
- Excretion: Excretion removes the waste products of metabolism.
- Growth: Growth is a permanent increase in size; making food supplies the materials for it, but is not growth itself.

questions.stem: Movement in green plants differs from movement in most animals because plants
questions.explanation:
Most animals show locomotion, moving the whole body. Plants are fixed, so their movements are slow movements of parts, mostly by growth.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- do not move at all: Plants do move: leaves turn towards light, flowers open and close, and tendrils coil round supports.
- move from place to place faster than animals: Rooted plants cannot move from place to place.
- move from place to place using their roots: Roots anchor a plant in one place; they do not carry it about.

options.label: B
options.content: move only parts of their bodies, such as leaves turning towards light, and do not move from place to place

options.label: C
options.content: move from place to place faster than animals

options.label: D
options.content: move from place to place using their roots

papers.title: Cell Structure: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on cell structure, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in a plant cell but NOT in an animal cell?
questions.explanation:
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole; animal cells have none of these.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Cell membrane: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane.
- Nucleus: Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus.
- Mitochondrion: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria for respiration.

questions.stem: The part of a cell that controls its activities and contains the chromosomes is the
questions.explanation:
The nucleus holds the chromosomes, which carry the genes that control the cell's activities.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cytoplasm: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like medium where most chemical reactions take place.
- vacuole: The vacuole stores cell sap and keeps a plant cell firm.
- chloroplast: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

questions.stem: The cell wall of a plant cell is made mainly of
questions.explanation:
Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which is strong and fully permeable.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- chitin: Chitin is found in the cell walls of fungi and the outer skeleton of insects.
- starch: Starch is stored food, not the material of the wall.
- protein: Protein is part of the cell membrane, not the main material of the wall.

questions.stem: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration in a cell?
questions.explanation:
Mitochondria release energy from food by aerobic respiration, so active cells have many of them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ribosome: Ribosomes make proteins.
- Chloroplast: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
- Golgi body: The Golgi body packages and secretes substances made in the cell.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms consists of only one cell?
questions.explanation:
Amoeba is unicellular: one cell carries out every life process.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Spirogyra: Spirogyra is a filament made of many cells joined end to end.
- Hydra: Hydra is a small animal made of many cells.
- Mushroom: A mushroom is a fungus made of many threads (hyphae) of cells.

questions.stem: Which part of a cell controls the movement of substances into and out of it?
questions.explanation:
The cell membrane is selectively (partially) permeable: it lets some substances through and holds others back.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Cell wall: The cell wall of a plant is fully permeable, so it lets almost everything through; it gives shape and strength.
- Nucleus: The nucleus controls the cell's activities through its genes, but substances enter and leave through the membrane.
- Vacuole: The vacuole stores cell sap; it does not control what enters the cell.

questions.stem: The large permanent vacuole of a plant cell
questions.explanation:
Cell sap is a solution of sugars, salts and other substances. When the vacuole is full of water, it presses the cytoplasm against the wall and keeps the cell turgid, which helps support the plant.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- contains the chromosomes: The chromosomes are in the nucleus.
- is the site of photosynthesis: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.
- makes proteins for the cell: Proteins are made on the ribosomes.

options.label: D
options.content: contains cell sap and keeps the cell firm (turgid)

papers.title: Photosynthesis and Plant Nutrition: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on photosynthesis and plant nutrition, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a product of photosynthesis?
questions.explanation:
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy trapped by chlorophyll.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is a raw material, taken in through the stomata.
- Water: Water is a raw material, absorbed by the roots.
- Chlorophyll: Chlorophyll traps light energy; it is needed for photosynthesis but is not a product of it.

questions.stem: The green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis is
questions.explanation:
Chlorophyll, in the chloroplasts, absorbs light energy and makes it available for photosynthesis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- haemoglobin: Haemoglobin is the red pigment in blood that carries oxygen.
- melanin: Melanin is the dark pigment in the skin of animals.
- starch: Starch is the food a plant stores; it is not a pigment.

questions.stem: When a leaf is tested for starch, it is placed in boiling alcohol (ethanol) in order to
questions.explanation:
Boil in water (kill the cells), boil in alcohol (remove the chlorophyll), rinse in warm water (soften), add iodine: blue-black shows starch.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- kill the cells and stop all chemical reactions: Boiling the leaf in water first does that.
- soften the leaf so the iodine can soak in: Dipping the leaf in warm water afterwards softens it; alcohol makes it brittle.
- change the starch into sugar: Alcohol does not change starch.

options.label: A
options.content: remove the chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen

options.label: B
options.content: kill the cells and stop all chemical reactions

options.label: C
options.content: soften the leaf so the iodine can soak in

questions.stem: A plant takes in most of the carbon dioxide it uses for photosynthesis through the
questions.explanation:
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the air into the leaf through the stomata, mostly on the lower surface.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- root hairs: Root hairs absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.
- xylem vessels: Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots.
- phloem sieve tubes: Phloem carries food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

questions.stem: Plants need magnesium because it is part of the molecule of
questions.explanation:
Magnesium sits at the centre of each chlorophyll molecule, so a plant short of magnesium turns yellow.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- protein: Proteins need nitrogen and sulphur, not magnesium.
- starch: Starch is made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.
- cellulose: Cellulose is also made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.

questions.stem: A variegated leaf (part green, part white) on a destarched plant is left in sunlight for six hours and then tested with iodine. Only the green parts turn blue-black. This shows that photosynthesis needs
questions.explanation:
The only difference between the green and white parts is chlorophyll. Starch formed only where chlorophyll was present, so chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- light: The whole leaf was in the light, so light was not the difference between the parts.
- carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide reached the whole leaf, so it was not the difference between the parts.
- water: Water reached the whole leaf through its veins, so it was not the difference between the parts.

questions.stem: Before an experiment on photosynthesis, a potted plant is destarched by
questions.explanation:
In the dark the plant cannot photosynthesise, so it uses up or moves away the starch in its leaves. Any starch found after the experiment must then have been made during it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- boiling its leaves in alcohol: Boiling a leaf in alcohol removes its chlorophyll during the starch test; it would kill the plant.
- watering it heavily for two days: Water does not remove the starch already in the leaves.
- keeping it in bright light for 48 hours: In bright light the plant would make more starch, not less.

options.label: B
options.content: keeping it in darkness for about 48 hours

options.label: C
options.content: watering it heavily for two days

options.label: D
options.content: keeping it in bright light for 48 hours

papers.topic: Food, Nutrition, and the Digestive System
papers.title: Food, Nutrition, and the Digestive System: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on food, nutrition, and the digestive system, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which food test gives a blue-black colour when the food is present?
questions.explanation:
Iodine solution turns from brown to blue-black when starch is present.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Benedict's solution with glucose: Glucose with Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate on heating.
- Biuret reagent with protein: Protein with Biuret reagent gives a purple (violet) colour.
- Ethanol with fat: Fat shaken with ethanol and then water gives a cloudy white emulsion.

questions.stem: A shortage of vitamin C in the diet causes
questions.explanation:
Without vitamin C, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly: the signs of scurvy. Fresh fruit such as oranges prevents it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rickets: Rickets is caused by a lack of vitamin D (or calcium).
- night blindness: Night blindness is caused by a lack of vitamin A.
- beriberi: Beriberi is caused by a lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine).

questions.stem: Digestion of protein begins in the
questions.explanation:
Pepsin in the gastric juice of the stomach begins the digestion of proteins, in acid conditions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- mouth: Starch digestion begins in the mouth, with salivary amylase; protein is not digested there.
- small intestine: Protein digestion continues in the small intestine, but it has already begun in the stomach.
- large intestine: The large intestine mainly absorbs water and salts.

questions.stem: Bile, which emulsifies fats, is made by the
questions.explanation:
The liver makes bile; it is stored in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gall bladder: The gall bladder stores bile, but does not make it.
- pancreas: The pancreas makes pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes.
- stomach: The stomach makes gastric juice.

questions.stem: Most digested food is absorbed into the blood in the
questions.explanation:
The ileum is long and lined with villi, which give a huge surface for absorbing digested food.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- stomach: Very little is absorbed in the stomach.
- colon: The colon absorbs mainly water and salts.
- oesophagus: The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach by peristalsis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme begins the digestion of starch in the mouth?
questions.explanation:
Salivary amylase starts to break starch down into maltose in the mouth. Pancreatic amylase continues the work in the small intestine.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Pepsin: Pepsin digests protein, in the stomach.
- Lipase: Lipase digests fats and oils into fatty acids and glycerol.
- Trypsin: Trypsin, from the pancreas, digests protein in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Roughage (dietary fibre) is important in the diet because it
questions.explanation:
Fibre, mainly cellulose from vegetables, fruit and whole grains, adds bulk, so the gut muscles can push the food along by peristalsis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- supplies most of the body's energy: Most energy comes from carbohydrates and fats; humans cannot digest fibre.
- is digested into amino acids: Amino acids come from the digestion of protein.
- builds strong bones and teeth: Strong bones and teeth need calcium and vitamin D.

options.label: A
options.content: supplies most of the body's energy

options.label: D
options.content: helps food move along the intestine and prevents constipation

papers.title: Cellular Respiration: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on cellular respiration, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which word equation shows aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation:
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen: That is photosynthesis.
- glucose → lactic acid + energy: That is anaerobic respiration in muscle.
- glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy: That is anaerobic respiration in yeast.

options.label: A
options.content: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

questions.stem: During hard exercise, which substance builds up in the muscles and causes fatigue and cramp?
questions.explanation:
When oxygen runs short, muscle respires anaerobically and lactic acid builds up; it is removed later, using oxygen.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ethanol: Ethanol is made by yeast and plants in anaerobic respiration, not by human muscle.
- Carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is carried away in the blood and breathed out.
- Glycogen: Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate used as fuel, not a waste.

questions.stem: Which gas turns lime water milky?
questions.explanation:
Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide, which is how the gas given off in respiration is shown.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Oxygen: Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
- Hydrogen: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.
- Nitrogen: Nitrogen has no effect on lime water.

questions.stem: Anaerobic respiration in yeast is used in
questions.explanation:
Yeast gives carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise, and ethanol, which is the alcohol in brewing.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- making yoghurt: Yoghurt is made by bacteria that produce lactic acid.
- smoking fish: Smoking preserves fish by drying it; yeast plays no part.
- producing antibiotics: Antibiotics such as penicillin come from the mould Penicillium, not from yeast fermentation.

questions.stem: Compared with anaerobic respiration, aerobic respiration of the same amount of glucose
questions.explanation:
Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely, so it releases far more energy than anaerobic respiration.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- does not need oxygen: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen; anaerobic does not.
- produces lactic acid: Lactic acid is made in anaerobic respiration in muscle.
- takes place only in plants: Aerobic respiration takes place in all living cells that have oxygen.

questions.stem: The energy released by respiration is transferred to a molecule that supplies energy for the activities of the cell. This molecule is
questions.explanation:
ATP carries energy in a form the cell can use straight away: for muscle contraction, active transport, making proteins and cell division.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- glucose: Glucose is the fuel that is broken down; the energy released is passed to ATP.
- glycogen: Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate in the liver and muscles.
- carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration and carries no useful energy.

questions.stem: After a race, an athlete keeps breathing deeply and quickly for some time. This is to
questions.explanation:
During hard exercise muscles respire anaerobically and lactic acid builds up. Afterwards, extra oxygen is used to break it down: this is the oxygen debt being repaid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- store extra oxygen in the muscles for the next race: The body cannot store extra oxygen for later in this way.
- get rid of the ethanol made in the muscles: Human muscle makes lactic acid, not ethanol.
- cool the body by breathing out heat: Breathing does lose a little heat, but it is not why breathing stays fast after exercise.

options.label: A
options.content: store extra oxygen in the muscles for the next race

options.label: B
options.content: take in the extra oxygen needed to remove the lactic acid made during the race (the oxygen debt)

options.label: C
options.content: get rid of the ethanol made in the muscles

options.label: D
options.content: cool the body by breathing out heat

papers.title: Transport in Plants: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on transport in plants, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Water and mineral salts are carried up the stem of a plant in the
questions.explanation:
Xylem vessels are long, dead, hollow tubes that carry water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- phloem: Phloem carries food made in the leaves.
- cambium: Cambium is a layer of dividing cells that makes the stem thicker.
- cortex: The cortex is a packing and storage tissue.

questions.stem: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant is called
questions.explanation:
Transpiration is the evaporation of water from the leaf cells and its loss as vapour through the stomata.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- translocation: Translocation is the movement of food in the phloem.
- guttation: Guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets, not vapour.
- osmosis: Osmosis is the movement of water from cell to cell across a membrane.

questions.stem: Which conditions would make a plant transpire fastest?
questions.explanation:
Heat speeds evaporation, dry air keeps a steep gradient, and wind carries away the moist air around the leaf.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Cold, humid and still: Cold, moist, still air slows evaporation.
- Warm but very humid: Humid air reduces the difference in water vapour between leaf and air.
- Dark, with the stomata closed: With the stomata closed, very little water vapour escapes.

questions.stem: Water enters the root hairs from the soil mainly by
questions.explanation:
The cell sap of a root hair is more concentrated than soil water, so water moves in by osmosis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- active transport: Active transport takes in mineral ions against a gradient, not water.
- transpiration: Transpiration is water loss from the leaves.
- phagocytosis: Phagocytosis is the engulfing of particles, as by white blood cells.

questions.stem: A ring of bark, including the phloem, is removed from a woody stem. Weeks later the bark just above the ring has swollen. This is because
questions.explanation:
This ringing experiment shows that food travels down the stem in the phloem.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- water moving up in the xylem collects above the ring: The xylem lies deeper and was not removed, so water still passes upwards.
- the xylem was removed with the bark: Only the bark and phloem were removed; the xylem is in the wood.
- the cells above the ring divide faster in the light: Light plays no part: the swelling is food that cannot move further down.

options.label: A
options.content: water moving up in the xylem collects above the ring

options.label: B
options.content: food moving down in the phloem collects above the ring

options.label: C
options.content: the xylem was removed with the bark

options.label: D
options.content: the cells above the ring divide faster in the light

questions.stem: Food made in the leaves is carried to other parts of the plant mainly as
questions.explanation:
Translocation moves sucrose and amino acids in the phloem, up and down the plant, to where they are used or stored.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- starch, in the xylem: Starch is insoluble, so it cannot be carried in solution; and the xylem carries water and minerals.
- glucose, in the xylem: The xylem carries water and mineral salts upwards, not food.
- starch, in the phloem: Starch is insoluble; sugar is carried in the phloem as soluble sucrose.

questions.stem: A potometer is used to measure
questions.explanation:
The distance an air bubble moves along the capillary tube in a set time shows how fast the shoot takes up water. Comparing conditions, such as still and moving air, shows what affects transpiration.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the rate of photosynthesis of the shoot: A potometer measures water movement, not photosynthesis.
- the amount of food carried in the phloem: A potometer cannot measure food movement.
- the exact amount of water lost by transpiration: It measures water uptake, which is only an estimate of transpiration, because some water is used by the shoot.

options.label: A
options.content: the rate of photosynthesis of the shoot

options.label: B
options.content: the amount of food carried in the phloem

options.label: C
options.content: the exact amount of water lost by transpiration

options.label: D
options.content: the rate at which a leafy shoot takes up water

papers.title: Ecosystems: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on ecosystems, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an abiotic factor in an ecosystem?
questions.explanation:
Abiotic factors are the non-living parts of the environment, such as rainfall, temperature, light and soil.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Predators: Predators are living organisms, so they are biotic factors.
- Decomposers: Decomposers are living organisms, so they are biotic factors.
- Parasites: Parasites are living organisms, so they are biotic factors.

questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, the bacteria that change ammonium compounds into nitrates are
questions.explanation:
Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, then Nitrobacter) turn ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates that plants can absorb.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- denitrifying bacteria: Denitrifying bacteria change nitrates back into nitrogen gas.
- nitrogen-fixing bacteria: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria change nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds.
- putrefying bacteria: Putrefying bacteria break down dead matter and release ammonia.

questions.stem: Organisms that break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil are called
questions.explanation:
Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down dead matter and release minerals for plants to use again.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- producers: Producers make food by photosynthesis.
- herbivores: Herbivores feed on living plants.
- parasites: Parasites feed on living hosts.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere by all of the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation:
Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air; respiration, burning and decay return it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- respiration: Respiration releases carbon dioxide.
- burning of fuels: Burning (combustion) releases carbon dioxide.
- decay of dead organisms: Decomposers respire as they break down dead matter, releasing carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: The flow of energy through an ecosystem begins with
questions.explanation:
Green plants trap light energy in photosynthesis; it then passes along food chains, with some lost at each step.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- decomposers breaking down dead matter: Decomposers receive energy at the end of food chains.
- herbivores eating plants: Herbivores are the second step: they eat what plants have made.
- carnivores eating herbivores: Carnivores come later still in the chain.

options.label: C
options.content: the sun's energy trapped by green plants

questions.stem: *Rhizobium* bacteria live in the root nodules of legumes. The bacteria get food from the plant, and the plant gets nitrogen compounds from the bacteria. This relationship is
questions.explanation:
Mutualism (symbiosis) benefits both partners. Lichens (a fungus with an alga) and the bacteria in the rumen of cattle are other examples.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- parasitism: In parasitism one partner benefits and the other (the host) is harmed.
- commensalism: In commensalism one partner benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.
- predation: In predation one animal kills and eats another.

questions.stem: Bare land left after a farm is abandoned is colonised first by grasses and weeds, then by shrubs, and finally by forest trees. This gradual change in the community is called
questions.explanation:
Each community changes the conditions (soil, shade, moisture) so that new species can establish, until a stable climax community, such as forest, develops.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- eutrophication: Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nutrients, which leads to algal blooms.
- competition: Competition between species is part of what drives succession, but it is not the name of the whole process.
- evolution: Evolution is the change in species over many generations, not the change of a community in one place.

papers.title: Mendelian Genetics: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on mendelian genetics, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Two tall pea plants, both heterozygous (Tt), are crossed. What ratio of tall to short plants is expected among the offspring?
questions.explanation:
Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt. Three have the dominant T, so 3 tall : 1 short.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1 tall : 1 short: A 1 : 1 ratio comes from crossing Tt with tt.
- 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt: That is the ratio of genotypes, not of tall to short plants.
- All tall: All tall offspring would come from crossing TT with any plant.

questions.stem: An organism with two identical alleles of a gene is said to be
questions.explanation:
Homozygous: two identical alleles, such as TT or tt.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- heterozygous: Heterozygous means having two different alleles.
- dominant: Dominant describes an allele that shows its effect even with one copy.
- recessive: Recessive describes an allele that is hidden when a dominant allele is present.

questions.stem: The observable characteristics of an organism, produced by its genes and its environment, are called its
questions.explanation:
The phenotype is what can be seen or measured, such as height or blood group.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- genotype: The genotype is the genetic make-up, such as Tt.
- allele: An allele is one form of a gene.
- chromosome: A chromosome is a thread of DNA that carries genes.

questions.stem: In humans, the sex of a baby is decided by
questions.explanation:
Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y: an X sperm gives a girl (XX), a Y sperm gives a boy (XY).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the sex chromosome carried by the mother's egg: Every egg carries an X chromosome, so the egg cannot decide.
- the number of eggs released: The number of eggs affects twins, not sex.
- the mother's diet during pregnancy: Diet does not decide the sex of a baby.

options.label: A
options.content: the sex chromosome carried by the mother's egg

options.label: C
options.content: the sex chromosome carried by the father's sperm

questions.stem: A man of blood group AB and a woman of blood group O have a child. Which blood groups could the child have?
questions.explanation:
The father gives A or B; the mother gives O. The child is AO (group A) or BO (group B).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- AB or O: AB needs an A and a B allele, but the mother can give only O; O needs O from both parents, but the father gives A or B.
- O only: The father always passes on A or B, so the child cannot be group O.
- A, B, AB or O: All four groups are possible only when the parents are, for example, AO and BO.

questions.stem: A man and a woman both have the sickle cell trait (genotype AS). What is the chance that their child will also be a carrier (AS)?
questions.explanation:
AS × AS gives AA, AS, AS and SS. Two outcomes in four are AS, so the chance is 1 in 2 (50%). The chance of SS, sickle cell disease, is 1 in 4 (25%) for each child, in every pregnancy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0%: Each parent can pass on either A or S, so a child can easily receive one of each.
- 25%: 25% is the chance that a child will have sickle cell disease (SS), or will be AA.
- 75%: 75% is the chance that a child will NOT have sickle cell disease (AA or AS).

questions.stem: To find out whether a tall pea plant is TT or Tt, it is crossed with a dwarf plant (tt). Some of the offspring are dwarf. The tall plant must be
questions.explanation:
In a test cross the unknown is crossed with a homozygous recessive. Tt × tt gives Tt and tt in a 1 : 1 ratio, so dwarf offspring prove that the tall parent carried t.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- TT (homozygous tall): TT × tt gives only Tt offspring, so all would be tall.
- tt (homozygous dwarf): A tt plant would itself be dwarf, not tall.
- impossible to tell from this cross: This cross, a test cross, is exactly how the genotype is found.

options.label: C
options.content: impossible to tell from this cross
